h: A writer is a citizen too: the pen's duty in defending the Constitution
dek: In his column 'Kabhi-Kabhar', Ashok Vajpeyi says that now that politics has entered every corner of life, a writer voicing political views is not straying from the work but fulfilling literature's moral duty.
body: People often ask why writers leave their work to speak on politics. Ashok Vajpeyi's answer is simple: writers are citizens too, and standing up fearlessly for certain values is literature's moral responsibility. When politics is interfering in faith, food, dress, festivals, education, entertainment and even sport, why should literature and the arts not answer back?

He recalls Muktibodh, who said more than fifty years ago that an artist's political activity can be a true artistic inspiration, because the artist steps in not for power or fame but to give human life a better direction. But a writer should not leave literature for party politics; the writer's field is literature itself, and it is there that the writer must also fight against politics.

According to the writer, the Hindutva vision of the ruling politics wants to change the Constitution, democracy, the social and economic order and education through lies, hatred, fear and violence, and this is an open campaign. Out of this concern, a gathering called 'Hum Bharat ke Log' (We the People of India) will be held in New Delhi on 28 November. Its appeal has been signed by people such as Ashis Nandy, Romila Thapar, T.M. Krishna, Naseeruddin Shah, Mridula Garg, Adoor Gopalakrishnan and K. Satchidanandan.

For Vajpeyi, the Constitution is the code of conduct for the state, a charter of citizens' rights, the path to the courts and the hope of people on the margins. He alleges that arrogance, the misuse of money and power, and haste without debate are blocking these roles, and that an unprecedented alliance of religion, the market and the media has formed.

The deepest point is about history. For the first time in India, the literature and art of the past seventy-five years were created within democracy and constitutional freedom. So when these are in crisis, the arts cannot stay silent or afraid; their unease is both natural and moral.
nazar: Just before Constitution Day, this column is a reminder that the freedom in which whole generations of Hindi and Urdu writers after Premchand have written does not survive on its own. In this time of names cut from voter lists, journalists' visas cancelled and hate campaigns, a writer's silence is also taking a side.

But the list of signatories is mostly well-known people from big cities. The real test will be whether this voice reaches the writers, folk singers and teachers in small towns who have neither a platform nor protection, and who are the first to face court cases.
sawal: How much should writers speak up for the Constitution under which they learned to write?
ref: Muktibodh
Gajanan Madhav Muktibodh (1917-1964), a major Hindi poet and critic. In poems such as 'Andhere Mein' (In the Dark) he wrote about power, fear and the responsibility of the intellectual.
Kabhi-Kabhar
Ashok Vajpeyi's long-running weekly column (the name means 'Now and Then'), in which he writes on literature, art and the politics of the times; it now appears in The Wire Hindi.
ank: Literature created within democracy and constitutional freedom
'Hum Bharat ke Log' gathering in Delhi
photo_note: Portrait of Rabindranath Tagore, by Abanindranath Tagore

h: Judges are citizens without papers, ordinary people suspects despite every paper
dek: In The Wire, Venkatesh Nayak uses RTI replies to show that no proof of citizenship is asked for when judges are appointed, while poor women in Assam are declared foreigners even after showing every document.
body: Venkatesh Nayak, director of the Commonwealth Human Rights Initiative, begins with two Gauhati High Court judgments. A tribunal had declared Jagyun Nesa of Barpeta a foreigner; the High Court upheld this because she could not firmly prove her date of birth, her link to her father and grandfather, a marriage three decades old and her continuous residence in Assam.

Kulchan Begum of Kamrup had her PAN and voter cards judged insufficient because they were made on her own application. Ration cards, voter lists and the fact that her father had been a ward member in the Guwahati Municipal Corporation did not help either. Bail was cancelled for both women.

Articles 124(3) and 217(2) say that a non-citizen cannot become a judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court. So is a judge's citizenship checked more strictly than an ordinary voter's? In August 2026 the writer filed an RTI (Right to Information) request. The Law Ministry pointed to the Memorandum of Procedure (MoP), and the Home Ministry said it has neither a process to check citizenship nor a list of firm documents.

That memorandum asks a High Court candidate for personal details, date of birth, school and college records and a health certificate, but not proof of citizenship. For the Supreme Court, only a health certificate is needed. In more than twenty files on the appointment of governors, too, the writer found no citizenship document.

His argument is that judges and governors are assumed to be citizens without papers, while ordinary people are made to prove that every paper is genuine, which goes against the equality of Article 14. He gives his own example as well: after he moved to Bengaluru, his parents' names were found missing from the list in the SIR, though his mother has been voting since the 1960s.
nazar: This article shows the citizenship debate in its true shape: the burden of suspicion is put not on those sitting at the top but on those standing at the bottom. The institutions that ask others for papers going back to their ancestors run on trust themselves, and that trust is never given to a woman in Barpeta.

In this time of the SIR, when crores of people across the country are being asked to prove they exist, the plain demand of equality is that the standard applied to judges and governors should also apply to ordinary citizens.
sawal: Why is a judge's citizenship taken on trust, but Jagyun Nesa's only on paper?
ref: Foreigners Tribunal
Quasi-judicial bodies set up in Assam that decide whether a person is Indian or a 'foreigner'. Here the burden of proof lies on the accused person.
MoP (Memorandum of Procedure)
The government document that sets out the process for appointing Supreme Court and High Court judges, accepted jointly by the government and the collegium.
photo_note: Ducks on the water, symbolic photo

h: Free bus rides for women: easy to promise, costly to run
dek: In ThePrint, Harilal Bhaskar writes that free bus travel for women is the right policy, but if governments do not pay for it on time, the buses themselves start to fall sick.
body: Announcing free bus travel for women is easy, but the cost of diesel, tyres, salaries and repairs falls on the transport corporation. Harilal Bhaskar of I-STEM, an initiative linked to the Office of the Principal Scientific Adviser, writing in a personal capacity, says the policy is not wrong; what is wrong is that its funding is not fixed.

The benefits are clear: the range for job-hunting widens, girl students can continue their studies and dependence on the family for fares goes down. According to studies cited from Tamil Nadu's transport department, women in Tiruppur, Madurai and Nagapattinam are saving 888 rupees a month on average.

The trouble is in payment. Under Karnataka's 'Shakti' scheme, the state owed four transport corporations 5,650.95 crore rupees as of August 2026. When money comes late, repairs are put off, trips are cut and crowding grows. Tamil Nadu treats it as a permanent public service, where the zero-fare tickets themselves become claims in the budget. Kerala and West Bengal started the facility in June.

The writer wants electronic ticket data to serve as proof of service, and a fixed monthly amount to be paid based on the real cost. He suggests that the corporation should get a share of earnings from medicine shops, food, ATMs, women's help desks and advertising at bus stations, and that industrial areas, IT parks and hospitals should share the cost of their routes.

A 2024 multi-state study found that bus costs fell, but no immediate rise in employment was seen, so he also argues for judging the policy on time, access and freedom. His advice is to run a year-long trial on three kinds of routes and publish the results along with the costs, or else the scheme will die in old buses and long waits.
nazar: Free bus travel is often brushed aside as a 'revdi' (a handout), when for a domestic worker, a woman in a factory or a girl going to college it is a question of the freedom to move. The real lesson of the article is that this right should be run not as an election gift but as a service tied to the budget.

The burden of unpaid dues finally falls on the very woman the scheme was made for: the bus comes late, comes full or does not come at all. But it is also not right to weigh public transport by earnings; nobody asks roads and flyovers to make a profit.
sawal: Which bus stop pays the price of Karnataka's 5,650 crore in dues?
ref: Shakti scheme
A Karnataka government scheme started in 2023 under which women can travel without a ticket in the state's government buses.
Public service obligation
A service that the government has run in the public interest despite losses, and whose cost it pays under set rules.

h: Equal incomes for all by 2100: the Piketty team's global map
dek: In Jacobin, Thomas Piketty, Lucas Chancel, Anmol Somanchi and colleagues write that every country can reach today's living standards of rich regions, provided energy changes, the rich consume less and wealth is widely shared.
by: Thomas Piketty, Lucas Chancel, Anmol Somanchi and others
body: Seven researchers of the World Inequality Lab, including Thomas Piketty and Anmol Somanchi, answer in this article the criticism of their 'Global Justice Report' of June 2026. They claim that by 2100 every region of the world can reach the average income of today's richest regions, and the Earth's temperature can still stay within the two-degree limit.

The starting picture is bitter. The average income of sub-Saharan Africa is one sixteenth of North America's, and the world's richest roughly 80 thousand people hold three times as much wealth as half of humanity.

In the writers' main scenario, the average monthly income of every person will be about five thousand euros by the end of the century. Poor regions will grow three to four percent a year and rich ones will stay almost still. The bottom half's share of wealth will rise from two percent to over thirty percent, and billionaires' share will fall from six percent to almost zero. About 90 percent of people will see their incomes double and their working hours halved.

This needs three things together: a fast energy transition, lower consumption and shorter working hours in rich countries, and large-scale sharing within and between countries. The proposal is a global justice fund, filled by a progressive tax on individuals' income and wealth across the world, which gives every country an equal share per person. Along with it is a call to end voting by money in the IMF and World Bank.

The writers admit that their model is rough and perhaps too slow. They put colonial and climate damage at more than twice today's world GDP, and cite the British 'Home Charges' imposed on India as an example, but they choose a forward path of equality over settling old accounts.
nazar: India stands on both sides of this debate: it was a colony that bore the 'Home Charges', and today it is among the world's most unequal societies, where a handful at the top hold a large share of wealth. If there is talk of a global tax on wealth, the same question will arise at home: how much tax do our own billionaires pay?
In climate talks India asks for the 'right to development'. This report says that right is real only when its benefit reaches the slum, the field and the mine, and not just the GDP figures.
sawal: Who will tax the wealth of eighty thousand people?
ref: World Inequality Lab
A research centre linked to the Paris School of Economics that collects data on income and wealth inequality around the world; Thomas Piketty and Lucas Chancel are associated with it.
Home Charges
Money sent from India to England under British rule, including officers' pensions, interest on debt and the cost of administration; Dadabhai Naoroji called it the 'drain of wealth'.
photo_note: A lone flower rising from the soil, symbolic photo

h: Apps, chatbots and queues: the state's work is now the public's burden
dek: In Jacobin, doctor Jatinder Hayre writes that institutions are pushing their work onto the public through apps, chatbots and phone menus, and the poor, the sick and the disabled pay the heaviest price.
body: Jatinder Hayre, a doctor by profession, starts with one of his patients. A test on a lump in the throat found cancer, but after that no appointment came and no doctor called. On paper every step was completed, yet nobody reached the patient. According to the writer, this is not a one-off slip but a deliberate design.

The writer takes forward Cory Doctorow's word 'enshittification', the state in which a platform, once it has become essential, worsens its terms. Hayre says this is now happening in public and essential services: hospitals, insurance and telecom have all hidden behind apps, online accounts and phone menus, taking full payment while making the customer do the work. He calls this 'socialised inconvenience', and calls the crowd of contractors, consultants and managers the 'processariat', in which everyone handles a piece of the process but nobody is responsible for the outcome.

The numbers show the cost. In a survey of 4,155 insured adults in the US, about a quarter said they delayed or skipped care because of paperwork, and the burden was heavier on disabled people. When Medicaid in Arkansas was tied to work and reporting conditions, 18 thousand people lost their insurance, while no rise in employment was seen.

The writer also gives an example from India. In Jharkhand, biometric identification for rations reduced corruption somewhat, but an estimated 15 to 20 lakh eligible people were denied rations at some point, largely because of the way the change was made. Hayre demands that public services have enough staff with the authority to solve problems, that getting one's rights should not take as much running around as a second job, and that institutions claiming 'savings' should also account for the labour they have pushed onto the public.
nazar: The Jharkhand example repeats every day in India: no fingerprint match, no ration; no OTP, no pension; server down, no MGNREGA attendance. In the praise of 'Digital India' it is often forgotten that for the elderly person, labourer or Adivasi (indigenous) person without a smartphone and network, every new app is a new wall.

The real test of welfare schemes should be how many eligible people were left out, not how many 'fake' names were cut. A responsible worker sitting at the counter is often more useful than the best technology.
sawal: When the fingerprint does not match, who is responsible for the hunger?
ref: Enshittification
A word coined by writer Cory Doctorow: digital platforms first attract users, then once they become essential, they worsen the service to squeeze out profit.
Aadhaar and rations in Jharkhand
Aadhaar-based biometric verification was made compulsory in Jharkhand's public distribution system; research and ground reports found large numbers of eligible people denied rations.

h: A test for the left in Spain: a rent crisis, and the far right at the door
dek: In The Nation, Sebastiaan Faber and Bécquer Seguín write that Pedro Sánchez, who has survived crisis after crisis, may lose power this time, and Spain may get a right-wing government with the far-right Vox.
body: According to the writers, Spain's progressive government may be in its final days. Pedro Sánchez came to power in 2018 through a no-confidence motion, the first in the country's history, and for the last three years has run a weak coalition government without a majority. In 2023 he held off an opposition with an eight-point lead, but this time things are different.

Polls show the right-wing Popular Party at about 31.5 percent and the far-right Vox at about 18 percent, which together would be past an absolute majority in the 350-seat parliament. By the writers' estimate, Sánchez's party has a one-in-four chance of winning the election and he has only a ten percent chance of staying prime minister. The forces to his left are scattered: the 15-party front of former Barcelona mayor Ada Colau looks set to get about ten seats, and Podemos perhaps one.

The writers list Sánchez's record: bringing the country through the Covid period, clashing with Trump, NATO and Israel over defence spending and Gaza, and making Spain the best performer among Europe's big economies. Yet housing has become the centre of the election debate. House prices have risen about 91 percent in the last ten years, and about 31 percent since 2024.

In September an elderly tenant in Madrid, whose building had been bought by a corporate landlord, was evicted for failing to pay rent. After the protests over this, Sánchez chose an early election. The writers say he is now betting on fear of the far right and the opposition's weak campaign, while the Vox leader cancelled an interview with a popular YouTuber at the last minute, after which the party fell about two points in the polls.
nazar: Spain's story shows that good economic numbers do not help when a roof over one's head keeps getting costlier for ordinary people. In India's big cities too, rent and eviction are a daily fear in the lives of migrant workers and students, but this rarely becomes an election issue.
Showing fear of the far right is not enough to stop it; a scattered left and politics without real relief only open the road for it.
sawal: When homes cost 91 percent more, which way will the vote go?
ref: Vox
Spain's far-right party, founded in 2013; known for opposing migrants, feminism and regional autonomy. Its leader is Santiago Abascal.
Pedro Sánchez
Leader of Spain's Socialist Party (PSOE) and prime minister since 2018; counted among the European leaders who openly criticise Israel over Gaza.

h: 'The Indian Question': the American right drops its mask of merit
dek: In The Nation, Kali Holloway writes that the American right, which until yesterday opposed affirmative action and civil rights in the name of 'merit', is now revealing its real racism by calling successful Indians a 'problem'.
body: Kali Holloway argues that the American right's talk of 'merit' was always a cover for white supremacy. Edward Blum, who has fought lawsuits against affirmative action, said openly in 2015 that he needed plaintiffs of Asian origin, and activists like Christopher Rufo praised Asian Americans because they could not be accused of racism.

According to the writer, hatred against Indians has grown fast since Trump's second win, and its centre is the H-1B visa, more than 70 percent of which are held by Indian citizens. According to a report by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, anti-South Asian posts on X rose 240 percent between January 2024 and June 2026. The US Department of Homeland Security itself posted an AI image in which a South Asian man named 'Mr Singh' was threatened to leave the country on his own.

Holloway lists more examples: far-right figure Nick Fuentes attacked leaders with wives of Indian origin, including Vice President JD Vance; Vivek Ramaswamy left social media after a flood of abuse; a Republican leader in Texas mocked a photo of mostly South Asian students, which some leaders condemned and others openly backed.

Most important is Rufo's podcast episode 'The Indian Question', which called the H-1B a means of cutting local people's wages and called Indians who are ahead in education a problem for white Americans. The writer points out that this title echoes the 'Jewish Question' and the 'Negro Question' of history, and cites W.E.B. Du Bois, who questioned the thinking that treats a whole people as a 'problem'. In her view, the right cares not about merit but about the racial hierarchy that Indians' success is shaking.
nazar: For those in India who kept celebrating Trump and his supporters as 'our own', this article is a mirror: the far right's hatred finally reaches whoever does not fit its racial picture.
The lesson is for home too. When Bengali-speaking workers or Muslims in India are targeted as 'infiltrators', the same poison is at work that Indians in America are now falling victim to.
sawal: Why is Delhi silent on the image threatening 'Mr Singh'?
ref: H-1B visa
A temporary US work visa given to skilled foreign professionals, especially in the IT sector; Indians are its biggest beneficiaries.
Affirmative action
A US policy of promoting Black and other disadvantaged groups in education and jobs; in 2023 the Supreme Court struck down its race-based use in university admissions.

h: UP voter list: more than a lakh voters older than their own parents
dek: An Alt News investigation found 1,10,875 entries in Uttar Pradesh's new draft list in which the listed father or mother is the same age as the voter or younger.
body: In the draft voter list of the Special Summary Revision (SSR) published in Uttar Pradesh on 17 November, Alt News has caught 1,10,875 entries in which the voter's father or mother is listed in the same house and the same booth, but is the same age as the voter or younger. In 35,523 of these cases the parent and child are the same age, in 75,352 the parent is younger, and in 6,860 the parent is twenty or more years younger.

These errors are spread across all 75 districts and 403 assembly constituencies. The most cases were found in Kushinagar district (3,646) and, by single seat, in Fazilnagar (711). One example is from Dhaulana in Hapur, where an 87-year-old voter's father is listed as 23. A 123-year-old woman's mother is listed as 45, and two women are shown as each other's mother.

For the investigation, machine-readable copies of the list were taken and each voter's listed parents were searched for in the same house number. The report recalls that in the SIR held earlier, the Commission's software was built to catch exactly this kind of 'logical discrepancy', such as parents being less than fifteen years older than the voter, and notices had even gone to about 2.22 crore people.
The draft list has 13.58 crore voters in all. Claims and objections can be filed until 16 December, and the final list is due on 4 January 2027. The report records no reply from the Commission.
nazar: In the name of the SIR, more than two crore names were cut in Uttar Pradesh and crores of people had to show papers as if proving their citizenship. If, in the list after that very drive, more than a lakh errors remain that a simple check would catch, the question is not how wrong the list is but on whom the burden of the weeding-out was placed. Poor voters were asked for documents, while the Commission's own mistakes sat in the list without accountability.
sawal: Who wrote down a 23-year-old father for an 87-year-old voter?
ref: SSR
Special Summary Revision: the regular yearly correction of the voter list. On 15 October 2026 the Commission ordered it to begin in 17 states and union territories including UP.
SIR
Special Intensive Revision: a drive to check the list afresh. In UP it ran from October 2025 to April 2026, and voters fell from 15.44 crore to 13.39 crore.

h: Form 7 case: probe against Jayanagar BJP MLA will go on
dek: The Karnataka High Court refused to stop the probe into an alleged attempt to get six Muslim voters' names deleted, but barred arrest and a chargesheet.
body: The Karnataka High Court has refused to stay the police probe against C.K. Ramamurthy, the BJP MLA from Bengaluru's Jayanagar seat, and three others. The allegation is that during the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) under way in the state, they tried to get the names of six Muslim voters removed from the list by filing fake Form 7s.
The court let the probe continue, but told the state government that the petitioners should not be arrested and no chargesheet should be filed against them without the court's permission.

The decision matters because in the past few weeks the High Court has stayed probes in several similar cases. According to a Bar and Bench report of 17 November, Justice Anant Ramanath Hegde had then stayed probes against ten people in three more FIRs, which took the number of such stayed cases to five. Those complaints mentioned thousands of Form 7 applications from Malleshwaram, Jayanagar, Yeshwantpur, Kodagu and Mysuru. The court's reasoning then was that the officer's inquiry under the voter registration rules should be completed first, and that different signatures alone do not prove forgery.

In those cases the state said that revision cannot be a licence for forged applications, while the accused argued that parties' booth agents can file objections through Form 7 and checking them is the election officer's job.
nazar: Form 7 is meant for objecting to a wrong name, not as a tool to push a community out of the list. When complaint after complaint shows Muslim voters as the target, it is not right to brush it off as a paperwork dispute. That the probe continues is a relief, but the real test will be whether charges against an elected representative are examined as seriously as an ordinary voter is asked for proof of identity.
sawal: Whose signatures were on the request to delete six names?
ref: Form 7
An application to object to a name in the voter list or have it removed. In many states there have been allegations of its bulk and fake use.
Registration of Electors Rules, 1960
The rules under which adding and removing names and hearing objections take place. The Electoral Registration Officer checks applications under these rules.

h: Facial recognition at Jantar Mantar: former CJIs raise questions
dek: At a debate in Delhi, former Chief Justices D.Y. Chandrachud and U.U. Lalit raised sharp questions about state surveillance and the limits of the right to privacy.
body: The topic of a debate held by a law firm in New Delhi on 22 November was whether the right to privacy should stop the state from using technology for surveillance. Among those giving the verdict were former Chief Justices D.Y. Chandrachud and U.U. Lalit and senior advocate and MP Abhishek Manu Singhvi.

Chandrachud set two uses of facial recognition side by side: finding pilgrims lost at the Maha Kumbh, and identifying protesters at Jantar Mantar, which Delhi Police reportedly did in July 2026. His question was whether the difference lies in the place, the purpose or the person, and whether a standing police order allowing videography of crowds also gives the right to identify every protester.

Speaking against the motion, senior advocate Rajiv Shakdher said such technology first needs a valid law, which India does not yet have, and that all surveillance must pass the three tests of the Puttaswamy judgment. C.A. Sundaram admitted that in the Puttaswamy case he had once argued for the government that privacy is not a fundamental right, and that he now considers that view a mistake. Nandita Rao said that mass surveillance can deepen inequality against women.

Speaking for the motion, Additional Solicitor Generals Chetan Sharma and Pinky Anand said privacy calls not for a ban on surveillance but for its regulation, and that the courts will keep watch on the government.
nazar: This is no longer a question for seminars. When the police can identify every face at a peaceful protest, without even a clear law for it, the price of joining a protest goes up. When two former Chief Justices of the country openly raise questions about this, the silence of Parliament and the courts stands out even more. The easier surveillance becomes, the more urgent a law to rein it in.
sawal: Why are a lost pilgrim and a protester the same to the camera?
ref: Puttaswamy judgment
In 2017 a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court held privacy to be a fundamental right. Any intrusion must meet the conditions of law, a legitimate aim and proportionality.
Facial recognition
Technology that identifies a person by matching faces in camera images. The debate heard that India lacks an adequate legal framework for it.
photo_note: A watchtower built around a tree on a hill, symbolic photo

h: Half the country in the grip of drought, rabi sowing lags behind
dek: According to IIT Gandhinagar's drought monitor, 47.2 percent of the country's area is dry or in drought, and rabi sowing is more than 11 percent below last year.
body: IIT Gandhinagar's India Drought Monitor found in data up to 18 November that 47.2 percent of the country's geographical area is dry or in drought. A week earlier the figure was 46.6 percent, which means the situation is not improving but getting worse. Soil moisture is below normal across large parts of western and southern India.

At the root is a weak monsoon. According to the weather department, rainfall across the country this time was about 13 percent below normal, the fourth driest monsoon since 2001. Karnataka's 35 percent shortfall was the worst in 55 years, Rajasthan's was 22 percent and Maharashtra's 19 percent. In Marathwada the shortfall was about 40 percent, and even more in districts like Solapur and Beed.

The effect is showing in the fields. By 13 November rabi (winter crop) sowing had covered 1.78 crore hectares, against 2.01 crore hectares at the same time last year. On rain-fed land, sowing depends on the moisture left by the monsoon, and this time that moisture simply is not there.

Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Rajasthan have declared many districts drought-hit, but according to the report the drought has spread far beyond these declared areas. IIT Bombay's forecast says drought will continue in many states until 6 December, and researchers are advising farmers to choose crops that need less water.
nazar: Drought does not reach government paper until a district declares it, and relief, crop insurance and loan breaks come only with that declaration. When scientific data shows drought has spread beyond the declared districts, what about the farmers and farm workers who live in districts where nobody has admitted drought? The lagging rabi sowing will reach the cities too in the coming months, as migration from villages and costlier grain.
sawal: Where does a farmer turn when his district has not been declared drought-hit?
ref: India Drought Monitor
A system at IIT Gandhinagar that measures drought across the country every week using satellite and ground data. It sorts areas into categories from mild to exceptional drought.
Rabi
Crops sown in winter, such as wheat, gram and mustard. In many areas they are sown relying on the moisture left in the soil after the monsoon.
photo_note: A dry-looking field on a hazy morning, symbolic photo

h: The underground flow of the Ganga and Brahmaputra is drying up
dek: According to an IIT Gandhinagar study, the water that rivers get from groundwater has clearly fallen over sixty years at about 30 percent of the country's river stations.
body: In rivers that keep flowing after the rainy season, much of the water seeps in from under the ground; this is called baseflow. A study by Rajesh Singh, Hiren Solanki and Vimal Mishra of IIT Gandhinagar looked at data from 1961 to 2021 for 227 stations in 18 large river basins. At about 30 percent of the stations this flow has clearly fallen, while it rose at only 8 percent.

In the Ganga basin, a fall was seen at almost every station. The main stream is flowing, but the small tributaries are drying up. Many stations on the Brahmaputra show the same. The sharpest falls were in the Sabarmati, Kaveri, Pennar and southern coastal basins. Basins in semi-arid regions are taking the hardest hit.

According to Vimal Mishra, reckless pumping of groundwater is a major reason. Changes in land use, the spread of cities, the cutting of forests, the running of dams and rising temperatures also have an effect, though the study shows links and does not give a firm cause for each place. The flow was found to be weaker still in El Niño years and during long breaks in the monsoon.

The researchers warn that if this trend continues, some rivers that flow all year today could become seasonal. In the dry months, drinking water, irrigation and the life of the river all depend on this flow.
nazar: We see rivers from above, but their breath comes from below the ground. Every new tubewell, every patch of land that is paved over, cuts that breath a little. The drying of tributaries hurts first the villages on their banks, fishers, herders and small farmers. River-saving schemes have stayed limited to ghats and cleaning, and without a groundwater policy they will remain incomplete.
sawal: Which river's share is each new tubewell drinking?
ref: Baseflow
The water in a river that comes not directly from rain but by slowly seeping in from groundwater stored under the ground. In the dry season the river survives on this.
El Niño
The warming of the Pacific Ocean whose effect in India often shows up as a weak monsoon and drought.
photo_note: The sun over a river, symbolic photo

h: Kala-azar in Uttarakhand: missing from the state's register, recorded at AIIMS
dek: Records obtained under the Right to Information show that 33 kala-azar patients from Uttarakhand reached AIIMS Delhi from 2016 to 2025, while the state had considered the disease gone from its soil.
body: Chair Talla village sits at a height of 1,100 metres, about 30 kilometres from Pauri. The road ends at a solar farm, and from there a twenty-minute walk down a stony path brings you to the village. About nine years ago, the case regarded as the state's last case of kala-azar was recorded here.

But records obtained under the Right to Information say something else. Kala-azar patients from Uttarakhand reached AIIMS in Delhi every year between 2016 and 2025, 33 in all. According to the report, cases are still turning up among people in the area.

The gap exists because the state's health mission collects data through ASHA and ANM workers, which goes from primary centres to the district and the state. AIIMS keeps its own separate register, so patients from the hills who are treated in Delhi never enter the state's count.

Kala-azar is a neglected tropical disease caused by a parasite and spread by the bite of an infected female sandfly, and without treatment it kills most patients. Until now it has been seen as a disease of Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh; Uttarakhand is not on that list.
nazar: Declaring a disease 'eliminated' is often a declaration about data, not about the ground. When the registers of two government institutions do not talk to each other, a patient from a remote hill village vanishes from the map, and a disease that is not counted gets no budget for testing, medicine or sandfly control. For poor families, it means a costly journey to Delhi.
sawal: Why were patients recorded in Delhi left out of Pauri's count?
ref: Kala-azar
Visceral leishmaniasis, a disease caused by a parasite in which fever, weight loss and an enlarged spleen are common. India had set the goal of eliminating it as a public health problem.
Sandfly
A tiny insect, smaller even than a mosquito, that breeds in damp, dark places and in cracks of mud walls. Its female spreads the kala-azar parasite.
photo_note: Deodars and bare branches in a hill town, symbolic photo

h: Sit-in against Shillong ropeway enters day 19, fight reaches the NGT
dek: To save the water sources of Lum Shyllong, the Joint Action Committee repeated its demand that the project be moved elsewhere, and got an appointment to meet the Governor.
ask: Move the ropeway project away from Lum Shyllong
body: The sit-in against the proposed Shillong Peak ropeway in Shillong, the capital of Meghalaya, entered its 19th day on Tuesday. The Joint Action Committee (JAC) opposing the project said clearly that the construction should be moved from Lum Shyllong to some other place. The committee's objection is about the effect on the environment of this site and on the water sources around it.

The committee's general secretary, Dr Linda Marbaniang, told reporters that documents backing their objections have been submitted. According to her, changes are being seen in the flow of the Umjasai spring. Many people at the sit-in have also complained of stomach trouble and headaches. The JAC has so far knocked on the doors of the National Green Tribunal, Chief Minister Conrad K. Sangma and Governor C.H. Vijayashankar, and its meeting with the Governor is fixed for 25 November.

Dr Marbaniang said that after earlier talks with the Chief Minister, they now want concrete steps, not more assurances. She also asked what use this route, linking Shillong Peak to the lower terminal, would be to ordinary people and patients, when other places could be more useful.
nazar: This is a question not of opposing development but of choosing the site. Before planting a tourism pylon in the catchment from which the city gets its water, the government should make its departments' assessments public. Women have been on the street for three weeks; an invitation to talks means something only if it keeps open the option of changing the site.
sawal: Is the hill for tourists or for a thirsty city?
ref: National Green Tribunal
A special tribunal set up in 2010 that hears disputes over the environment, forests and pollution, and can also halt projects.
photo_note: Cattle grazing among green hills, symbolic photo

h: Bikram farmers hold sit-in, allege corruption at circle office
dek: The Bharatiya Kisan Sangh held a one-day sit-in at the block headquarters with a 19-point charter of demands, with stuck land-record and compensation cases at its centre.
ask: Clear land-record mutation cases quickly, and make compensation fair
body: Farmers held a one-day sit-in under the banner of the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh at the Bikram block headquarters in Patna district on Monday. The farmers came with a 19-point charter of demands, with stuck land cases at the top.

The farmers' main demand is that pending cases of dakhil-kharij (mutation of land records) and parimarjan (correction of records) be settled quickly. They say there should be a fair review of land acquisition and the compensation paid for it. They also asked for transparency in the circle office and a system to solve every problem within a fixed time. At the sit-in, corruption in the circle office was also alleged, with a warning that the agitation would grow if the demands were not met.

The sit-in was presided over by Arun Kumar and conducted by Shyam Kishore Sharma. According to the report, a large number of local farmers took part, but no count was given. As the sit-in was ending, Block Development Officer Pankaj Kumar arrived, spoke to the farmers and assured them their problems would be solved soon. No deadline or concrete promise is mentioned.
nazar: In Bihar's villages, land disputes are often stuck not in the field but in the files of the circle office. Making rounds for months for a mutation is a common complaint here. An assurance without a deadline only tells farmers to wait until the next sit-in.
sawal: How many sit-ins does it take to correct one land record?
ref: Dakhil-kharij
The process of entering a new owner's name in government revenue records after land is sold or inherited, also called mutation.
photo_note: A lone tree on dry land, symbolic photo

h: Farmers sit in at Khatauli tehsil, demand 600 for sugarcane
dek: The Kisan Mazdoor Sangathan held a sit-in outside the SDM's office and handed over a memorandum addressed to the Chief Minister; the high-handedness of the electricity department was also an issue.
ask: Announce a sugarcane price of 600 rupees a quintal
body: In Khatauli tehsil of Muzaffarnagar district in western Uttar Pradesh, workers of the Kisan Mazdoor Sangathan arrived on Monday packed into tractor-trolleys and sat in protest outside the SDM's office. Amid slogans, they made the SDM sit among them too, and made serious allegations against the tehsil staff. The report does not give details of these allegations.

The biggest demand in the memorandum addressed to the Chief Minister is to announce the sugarcane price and set it at 600 rupees a quintal. The farmers also asked for a fair survey of crops ruined by disaster and compensation, an end to the electricity department's high-handedness, and relief from faulty meters and raised loads. The memorandum also asks for an allowance for unemployed young people, Ayushman cards for people over 60, and payment of farmers' dues with interest.
The sit-in was presided over by Anangpal and conducted by Manoj Rana. The SDM gave an assurance that the problems would be solved, after which the memorandum was handed to him.
nazar: The crushing season has begun and sugarcane farmers still do not know at what price their crop will sell. The delay in announcing the price and the lack of interest on old dues together make the farmer an interest-free lender to the mill. The sit-ins at the tehsil are the price of this delay.
sawal: The crop has been cut, so why has the price still not been fixed?
ref: State Advised Price (SAP)
The sugarcane price the state government sets each crushing season. In Uttar Pradesh, mills are bound to pay farmers this price.
photo_note: The sun setting behind trees, symbolic photo

h: ASHA workers' sit-in in Bengaluru enters day eight, appeal rejected
dek: Standing firm on their demand for a monthly honorarium of 15 thousand rupees, ASHA workers said the protest will end only when the Chief Minister comes himself and issues the order.
ask: Fix ASHA workers' monthly honorarium at 15 thousand rupees
body: The round-the-clock indefinite sit-in of Karnataka's ASHA workers at Freedom Park in Bengaluru entered its eighth day on Tuesday. The protest was started on 17 November by the Karnataka State Samyukta ASHA Karyakartheyara Sangha, linked to the AIUTUC. Their main demand is that the monthly honorarium be fixed at 15 thousand rupees and that their other pending demands also be met.

Chief Minister D K Shivakumar, who is on a visit to Japan, spoke to the protest leaders on a video call while travelling on a train and appealed to them to end the sit-in. He assured them he would discuss their demands with the finance department during the assembly session and meet the workers on his return. He had made a similar appeal on 21 November too. He also accused the opposition of using the workers for political gain.

The union said clearly that the protest will not stop until the Chief Minister comes to the protest site himself and issues an order accepting the demands. Umamani, general secretary of an independent body of anganwadi workers, gave her support and said ASHA, anganwadi and mid-day meal workers should not be set against each other. Actor Mukhyamantri Chandru asked why Karnataka cannot pay when neighbouring Kerala can pay 12 thousand, while 20 crore is being spent on the Bengaluru Habba festival.
nazar: The women who carry the load of vaccination, childbirth and disease surveillance in every village have been under the open sky for eight days, and in reply they are getting assurances on a video call. For a government that finds money for a festival right away, the ASHA honorarium is not a file in the finance department but a question of intent.
sawal: How long can the backbone of the health system be called 'volunteers'?
ref: ASHA (Accredited Social Health Activist)
Village-level women health workers created in 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission. They get no salary, only task-based incentives and a state honorarium.
photo_note: A sapling tied to a wooden support, symbolic photo

h: Narsinghpur sugarcane farmers dig in at Bhopal, demand 600 rupees a quintal
dek: Rejecting the government's offer of 450 rupees, farmers are spending nights in the open on Hoshangabad Road and have warned they will march to the Chief Minister's residence.
place: Hoshangabad Road, Bhopal (farmers from Narsinghpur district)
ask: Sugarcane price of 600 rupees a quintal, plus a 50-rupee bonus
body: Sugarcane farmers from Madhya Pradesh's Narsinghpur district have been camped since Monday night on the service road near Veer Savarkar Setu on Hoshangabad Road in Bhopal. The farmers spent the night under the open sky and arranged their own food. They demand that the sugarcane price be raised from 400 rupees to 600 rupees a quintal, with a bonus of 50 rupees a quintal on top.

The government has offered 450 rupees a quintal, which the farmers rejected, saying it does not even cover the cost of farming. On Monday a delegation of five farmers met Agriculture Director Umashankar Bhargava, but the talks were inconclusive. Farmer leaders Prateek Sharma and Rakesh Dhakad announced that if no decision came by 2 pm, they would march towards the Chief Minister's residence. More farmers were expected to arrive by train and private vehicles.

Meanwhile, the police deployed about 45 personnel at night, including two DSPs and four inspectors, with the number set to reach 150 during the day. Barricades were put up at both ends of the service road. No formal statement has come from the government.
nazar: When farmers come to the capital to ask a price for their produce, barricades and police tents go up first, and talks come later. If there were a transparent system to fix the sugarcane price based on cost, farmers would not have to spend nights on the road.
sawal: Who should fix the cost, the one in the field or the one in the office?
ref: State advised price for sugarcane
The Centre sets the minimum fair and remunerative price (FRP) for sugarcane. Many states announce their own advised price above it, which sugar mills must pay farmers.

h: 'Matka phod' in Beed: 1,800 crore spent, still 421 tankers
dek: Despite claims of heavy spending on the Jal Jeevan Mission, 268 villages in the district depend on tankers, and RTI activists have demanded an independent audit.
ask: A probe and independent audit of Jal Jeevan Mission works
body: In Maharashtra's Beed district on Monday, activists broke clay pots outside the district collectorate in a 'matka phod' (pot-breaking) protest. They allege that according to officials, 1,800 crore rupees have been spent on the Jal Jeevan Mission in the district, yet a severe water shortage remains. Even today about 6.32 lakh people in 268 villages and 259 hamlets depend on 421 tankers.

The protest was led by Ganesh Dhawale Limbaganeshkar, publicity head of the Maharashtra State Right to Information Activists' Federation. A memorandum was sent through the collector to Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis, Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde, Guardian Minister Sunetra Pawar and Water Supply Minister Gulabrao Patil. The demand is for a full probe into how the scheme was carried out, strict action against guilty contractors and officers, and an independent audit of every approved work, actual spending, completion certificates, working tap connections and payments made to contractors.

The protesters asked whether many works were completed only on paper and whether anyone had gone to the sites to check quality. Many people took part, including Shaikh Yunus, Sarfaraz Pathan and Ashok Yede. The report records no reply from officials or ministers.
nazar: The promise of a tap in every home sounds hollow when, in the same district, six and a quarter lakh people wait for tankers. Asking for an account of such a large sum should have been the government's own job, not a protest's; here the burden is falling on RTI activists.
sawal: Why did the water flowing on paper never reach the village?
ref: Jal Jeevan Mission
A central scheme launched on 15 August 2019. Its goal is to give every rural home a tap connection supplying 55 litres of clean water per person a day.
photo_note: A single drop of water on a taro leaf, symbolic photo

h: Three years after the Teesta flood, relief camps are still home
dek: In Kalimpong, families uprooted by the 2023 glacial lake flood still live under tarpaulin and tin, while the river comes closer to them every year.
body: When Sikkim's South Lhonak lake burst in October 2023, the Teesta flood turned the lives of about eighty thousand people upside down. At Teesta Bazaar in Kalimpong, 36-year-old Bijay Pradhan lost his house, fields and cattle. Now he supports his family with daily-wage work and lives in a relief camp with hundreds of others.

The flood brought so much silt that, according to a central committee, the riverbed here rose by six to fourteen metres, and floods came again in 2024-25. Bhawani Boju, 66, has given up repairing her house, because the river that was several minutes away is now a minute away. Thirty-two families uprooted from Melli live in tarpaulin-and-tin homes on forest land along the highway, where snakes and rats get in and the fear of eviction stays.

Early assessments put about 550 houses as destroyed, but in a later survey the count fell to about 115, and people say many families were left out. A fully destroyed house gets 75 thousand rupees. After a fresh survey a plan was made for 116 houses, which was stuck in the state finance department as of September 2026.

Sikkim gave rent support and approved 4,100 houses, but West Bengal never declared the 2023 flood a disaster. So Kalimpong got one-time compensation, with no rent and no housing scheme. The MP blames the state, and the state blames the Centre. The report also says that warning sensors had never been installed on the lake.
Kopila, 56, who lost her camping business, now runs a small canteen, and the family is paying off loans. Bijay Pradhan is still in the camp, waiting for a lasting solution.
nazar: This story shows that a climate disaster in the Himalayas is not just one night of ruin but years of homelessness. When even declaring a disaster gets stuck in a tug-of-war between the Centre and the state, the first to be left out are those who have neither a land title nor a voice. Amid the race for dams and roads on the Teesta, the safety and resettlement of riverside villages should be the first condition, not an afterthought.
sawal: Whose responsibility are the homeless of a flood that was never called a disaster?
ref: Glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF)

A flood that comes when the natural dam of a lake formed by melting glaciers suddenly breaks.
This is what happened on the Teesta when Sikkim's South Lhonak lake burst in October 2023.
Gorkhaland Territorial Administration (GTA)

A semi-autonomous administration set up in 2012 for the Darjeeling and Kalimpong hill areas.
Many local development and relief tasks are its responsibility.
photo_note: A house surrounded by water, symbolic photo

h: Among Abu Abraham's lines: a walk with Om Thanvi and Apoorvanand
dek: In this conversation for The Wire, senior journalist Om Thanvi and Professor Apoorvanand walk through the work of cartoonist Abu Abraham, recognising the fearless art that questioned power with a laugh.
body: This is an introduction to The Wire's video conversation in which Delhi University professor Apoorvanand and senior journalist Om Thanvi walk through the work of cartoonist Abu Abraham. According to The Wire's description, the two examine the fearless, sharp-edged art that marked Abu's whole career.

Abu Abraham (1924-2002) was born in Kerala and is counted among the greatest voices of Indian newspaper cartooning. He drew for London's 'The Observer', then for 'The Indian Express' and 'The Statesman', and was also a member of the Rajya Sabha for some years. His cartoon from the Emergency, in which the President signs an ordinance while taking a bath, is still remembered today.

Deshkaal is not giving details here of which cartoons came up in the conversation or what was said at which point. What is written on this page is based on The Wire's description and on well-known facts about Abu Abraham. The conversation itself can only be had by watching it.

In his centenary year, a large exhibition of about three hundred original cartoons by Abu Abraham was held in Kochi, put together by his daughters Ayesha and Janaki. Such an account of his work is rarely seen, and this conversation seems to be a link in that same wish.
nazar: The cartoon is the form in which the room to laugh at power is the first to shrink. A conversation on Abu's lines between two people who are themselves known for asking questions is a reminder that laughter too can be a kind of fearless statement.
sawal: Would the cartoons once taken with a laugh still get printed today?
ref: Abu Abraham
Kerala-born cartoonist (1924-2002) who worked for The Observer, The Indian Express and The Statesman.
Om Thanvi
Senior journalist and former editor of 'Jansatta'.
Apoorvanand
Delhi University professor and social and political commentator.
photo_note: A scene from the conversation

h: Shakti Chattopadhyay: he did not just live life, he shaped it
dek: A day before his birthday, in Hindwi's 'C/O Bengal' series, Baby Shaw writes on the life and poetry of the bohemian Bengali poet Shakti Chattopadhyay.
body: Baby Shaw's essay begins with Shakti Chattopadhyay's famous poem in which the speaker weighs the idea of going back and finally refuses to go alone, unprepared. The writer says it is hard to understand Shakti through his poems alone, because his restlessness, friendships, adda (hangout) circles, loneliness and disarray had also become part of his identity as a poet. Yet this disarray never weakened the tightness of what he wrote.

The essay also maps his life. Born on 25 November 1933 in Joynagar in South 24 Parganas, he came to Bagbazar in Kolkata in 1948, leaned towards Marxism at sixteen, joined the Communist Party in 1951 and broke from it in 1958. Poverty forced him to leave Presidency College in 1956. His poem appeared in Buddhadeva Bose's magazine 'Kavita', then came years in Chaibasa with his friend Samir Roychoudhury, and his joining and breaking with the Hungry Generation movement.

His first collection, 'He Prem, He Noihshobdo' (O Love, O Silence), came out in 1961; the writer sees it as steeped in nature and love. The very title of 'Dhorme Achho Jirafeo Achho' (You Are in Religion, and in the Giraffe Too) puts religion and a giraffe side by side and questions inherited beliefs. In 1987, in Anandabazar Patrika, he asked why there were so many poets, and the literary world flared up.

The essay has stories too: he set out for the market with a bag and came back after wandering about a month in Darjeeling and the Dooars, while his family had already filed a missing person report. He changed the name of his first book several times and even changed poems at the proof stage. In 1995 he went to teach at Visva-Bharati, and that same year he died of a heart attack in Santiniketan.
nazar: Hindi readers often know Bengali poetry only up to Rabindranath and Jibanananda. A series like 'C/O Bengal' opens up the ground in between, where poets like Shakti kept searching for their freedom between the party, the magazine and the adda. Such traffic between languages is what keeps our shared literary heritage alive.
sawal: What did the poet who left with a bag bring back a month later?
ref: Hungry Generation
A Bengali literary movement started in 1961 by Malay Roychoudhury and his companions, which openly challenged established literary decorum. It also faced court cases.
Krittibas
A Bengali poetry magazine started in the 1950s by Sunil Gangopadhyay and his companions, which became an important platform for poets of the new generation.
photo_note: The swan messenger

h: A reel, a song and Gyanranjan at ninety
dek: Shirish Khare's essay asks why a story writer and a film star live side by side inside one reader.
body: One night, scrolling through reels on Facebook, Shirish Khare hears a young man sing 'Apna Dil To Awara' from 'Solva Saal'. Dev Anand is nowhere in the reel, there is only new music, yet his finger stops and the same face returns to his mind. This essay was written on Gyanranjan's ninetieth birthday, and the writer admits he cannot quite explain why these two names sit side by side within him.

As a child he watched 'Teen Deviyan' on a black-and-white TV, and Dev Anand has been with him since then. In his late teens he came upon Gyanranjan's 'Shesh Hote Hue' (While Coming to an End), and from the very first pages he felt this was written by someone who knew exactly what he was doing. Since then, whenever someone mentions Gyanranjan, the writer stops to listen.

His view of Gyanranjan is clear: few stories, great impact. His stories hold a young man's anger that does not scream but stays pressed down like coal under ash. The prose is so tight that if you remove one word, the sentence wobbles. As editor of 'Pahal' he gave space to many voices. That world from Allahabad to Jabalpur, where books and debate were the daily air, was not the writer's own world.

Dev Anand's world of English-speaking gatherings and shining cars was not his either. The writer argues that distance itself deepens the pull: anger in one, romance in the other, both perhaps within himself. He was glad to learn that Suraiya is mentioned in one of Gyanranjan's stories. In the end he says he does not want to become like either of them: let the song be someone else's, but the voice his own.
nazar: In Hindi, 'high' literature and 'light' cinema have long been kept in separate boxes. This essay quietly breaks that division and reminds us that an ordinary reader's sensibility is shaped by stories and songs together. Even in the age of reels, if a song can lead someone to 'Shesh Hote Hue', that is cause for hope.
sawal: How does anger pressed under ash survive in a story?
ref: Gyanranjan
Well-known Hindi story writer, known for stories such as 'Pita' (Father), 'Ghanta' (The Bell) and 'Bahirgaman' (Exit). He brought out the literary magazine 'Pahal' from Jabalpur for many years.
Suraiya
Singer and actor of the 1940s and 50s. She made several films with Dev Anand, and stories of their unfulfilled love are still famous.
photo_note: The hero and the milkmaid's scarf, Pahari miniature

h: Arundhati Roy: my mother was a tyrant, and a visionary too
dek: On Arundhati Roy's birthday, Sammukh has published a long conversation with her together with a Dutch writer's ode about fireflies.
by: Jitendra Kumar, Marjolijn van Heemstra (tr. Bharatbhushan Tiwari)
body: This presentation has two parts. In the first, Jitendra Kumar talks to Arundhati Roy about the Hindi translation of her memoir, 'Meri Maa, Meri Gangster' (My Mother, My Gangster), translated by Prabhat Singh and published by Rajkamal. The book is about her mother Mary Roy, who ran a school in Ayemenem in Kerala and fought against the inheritance law that discriminated against Syrian Christian women.

Roy says readers wrongly assumed that Ammu in 'The God of Small Things' was based on her mother. She calls this book a love story of two public women who were also mother and daughter. Her mother had severe asthma and any clash could bring on an attack, so the two could not speak openly. At home she was a tyrant, and outside a visionary. There is also talk of leaving home at sixteen, studying architecture in Delhi and not seeing her mother for about seven years.

She calls the word 'gangster' an affectionate one, a name for her mother's fighting spirit. The talk covers the Narmada movement, the nuclear tests, communal violence, and even going to jail for contempt of court. She rejects simple formulas like women good, men bad, because it was her brother who bore the most of their mother's anger. Despite the fear of lawsuits, she refuses to censor herself.

The second part is an ode by Dutch writer Marjolijn van Heemstra, translated by Bharatbhushan Tiwari. Its central image is the firefly: Pasolini saw the faint light of fireflies against fascist searchlights, and according to the writer, Roy's writing is that kind of light, which does not pull us towards some dazzling utopia but keeps us grounded in this very moment.
nazar: Mary Roy's inheritance case was a fight for equality for the Christian women of Kerala, and this conversation shows how tangled that fight was inside the home. Being able to see public courage and private harshness together is the honesty of this book and this conversation.
sawal: In an age of searchlights, who sees the firefly's light?
ref: Mary Roy case
In 1986, on Mary Roy's petition, the Supreme Court ruled that Syrian Christian women in Kerala would have rights to their father's property equal to sons.
Pasolini and the fireflies
In a 1975 essay, Italian poet and filmmaker Pier Paolo Pasolini made the disappearance of fireflies a metaphor for the spread of consumerist fascism.
photo_note: Daddy has come

h: The waxing moon of baldness: Lakshmi, the moon and the marriage market
dek: Gagan Talreja's satire uses falling hair to laugh at fake sympathy, the treatment business, and the thinking that sees marriage as the cure for every ill.
body: Gagan Talreja of Lucknow is a software engineer in Hyderabad who writes satire in his spare time. The very title, 'Ek Shukla Paksh Yah Bhi' (This Too Is a Waxing Moon), is a dig: the moon grows, and so does the shining patch on the narrator's head. He says he now has as much hair left on his head as a Hindi writer gets in royalties.

The real target is not hair but people. Acquaintances express sympathy, in which pity is mixed with relief that it did not happen to them. Relatives console him that bald men have more money in their pockets. The narrator replies with such exaggeration that the absurd layers of such advice peel open on their own.

In a dream, his falling hair turns into banknotes and fills his pockets. From this he builds a funny 'theory' about Lakshmi and the moon: the moon is Lakshmi's younger brother, so why would a sister leave her parents' home so soon for the house of a man with a shining head? Then comes the turn of the hair-growth industry, which feeds on men's insecurity: medicines, oils, shampoos, homoeopathy, all were tried.

The sharpest part comes at the end. The skin doctor gives him medicine and says to keep taking it until the wedding. From here the satire turns on the marriage market, where young men and women are like old buses dressed up for sale and parents call out for passengers like conductors. The narrator decides that his baldness will be put off until the wedding.
nazar: Beneath its light touch, this satire catches a serious point: in our society, worry about looks becomes a business when tied to the marriage market, and now men too carry this burden. A society that sees marriage as the cure for every trouble does not really listen to any trouble at all.
sawal: Why medicine 'until the wedding', and not after?
ref: Shukla paksha
In the Hindu calendar, the fifteen days from the new moon to the full moon, when the moon seems to grow each day.
Lakshmi and the moon
In mythology, both Lakshmi and the moon emerged from the churning of the ocean, so the moon is called Lakshmi's brother.
photo_note: Goddess Lakshmi

h: A cold table, the sound of boots and a lock on the tongue
dek: Ten short poems by Urdu fiction writer Ashar Najmi record the fear that power leaves without a mark, the silence, and the small acts of witness against it.
body: Mumbai-based Ashar Najmi is a well-known Urdu fiction writer. According to Samalochan's introduction, his 2021 novel 'Usne Kaha Tha' (He Had Said) was considered the first postmodern novel in Urdu, 'Shunya ki Tauheen' (An Insult to Zero) and 'Congress House' have come out in Hindi translation, he wrote TV serials for about two decades, and since 2008 he has brought out the Urdu magazine 'Isbaat'. Samalochan has published ten of his poems, whose language has the flow of Urdu and an economy of words.

The first two poems are about violence that leaves no mark on the body. In one, a shining table and the same question every morning at eight wear a man down, where the greatest cruelty is proving one's name every day. In the second, the sound of boots from years ago has settled in so deep that now even the rattle of the door latch makes the spine shiver.

Some poems are about bearing witness: the man who sticks posters on closed shops at three in the morning, knowing they will be scraped off by morning, yet sticks them so it is recorded that someone was awake in the dark. A broken pair of glasses lying on the road after a stampede, with tear gas smoke in one lens and a careless bird sitting on a pole in the other.

The other poems are about indifference and fear: a white kurta hanging untouched by dust, the round stain of a tea cup on a newspaper photo of a ruined home, a big face hung at the crossroads from which people avert their eyes, a mother who changes the ending of a story. The last poem is about a woman who breaks the lesson of staying silent and says a raw word on the street, and the men's decorated hall cracks.
nazar: These poems name no country or government, but the fatigue of proving one's identity every day is familiar to many in today's India. The tea stain reminds us that oppression runs not only on those who commit it, but also on those who fold the newspaper and move on.
sawal: Who put the tea cup on the newspaper photo?
ref: Isbaat
An Urdu literary magazine published from Mumbai, edited by Ashar Najmi since 2008.
Postmodern novel
A novel that questions a straight narrative, a single truth and the authority of the author, and often tells its story in many voices and fragments.
photo_note: A military officer of the East India Company, Company style

h: Sonia Gandhi's 'Belonging': a longing to be accepted, and party publicity
dek: Mahesh Kumar's review praises the family parts of Sonia Gandhi's autobiography, but calls the political parts Congress publicity.
body: Mahesh Kumar begins his review with memories of his youth, when rumours went around about Sonia Gandhi that a foreign-born leader could not become prime minister. The claim that the child of a foreign mother cannot be a patriot spread through speeches and social media, and fact-checks found it false. According to the reviewer, it was these very attacks that put 'belonging', the longing to be naturally accepted into a group, at the centre of the book.

He says this autobiography is less political and more about family. It holds the story of a childhood in a middle-class Italian family, love with Rajiv Gandhi and settling into an Indian home. The reviewer finds it notable that Rajiv got by during his student days by selling ice cream and doing manual work, and never took advantage of being the prime minister's son. He also praises the warmth with which the household staff are remembered, and calls the part about being accepted in Amethi moving.

On politics the reviewer is stern. The book lists the Congress's achievements, from the IITs, AIIMS and technology policy to Sanjay Gandhi's five-point programme, and is sharp on the BJP and RSS, while being soft on allies such as Mamata Banerjee, Lalu Prasad and Mulayam Singh.

His objection is that events have been chosen to suit the party's image. The defence on Bofors is weak, there is more criticism of Jayaprakash Narayan than of the Emergency, and the book is silent on the destruction of forests and the exploitation of Adivasis and the deprived under Congress rule. So, where the party is concerned, he sees Sonia Gandhi less as a writer and more as a publicist.
nazar: A woman's struggle to be accepted in a foreign land is a comment on the politics that measures loyalty by place of birth. But the reviewer rightly asks why an autobiography that speaks of its own pain is silent on the pain of the Adivasis whose land was taken under this party's rule too.
sawal: The longing to belong or loyalty to the party: whose book is it?

In 1986, allegations of kickbacks arose in the purchase of guns from the Swedish company Bofors, which became a major political crisis for the Rajiv Gandhi government.
